parsed.explanation: The division itself is protective: gender-identity discrimination is codified, hate-crime law covers gender identity explicitly, the panic-defence bar and conversion-therapy ban operate, and a July 2026 assessment places it in a low-risk tier. No division-specific facility ban, custody incident or violence data is documented. But the combined regime includes federal layers the division cannot displace: birth-sex exclusion from federally funded single-sex facilities (airports, federal buildings), visa instructions to refuse where documents cast doubt on sex with possible lifetime fraud findings, foreign-government advisories over document rules, security-screening outing risk, and documented conversion-style policy in federal corrections plus abuse in immigration custody. Litigation makes these volatile, not absent. Net: elevated risk — above service-friction jurisdictions, below those with no universal federal exclusion.

entry_documents.exposure: Jan 2025 order and Nov 2025 Supreme Court clearance bar non-binary/mismatched passport markers; Feb 2025 cable tells officers to refuse where documents cast doubt on sex and to weigh a lifetime fraud bar; travellers report blocked/confiscated passports and eight-plus foreign governments issued advisories over identity-document rules.
entry_documents.protection: Pre-existing 'X' passports remain valid until expiry; the marker suit and related challenges remain pending in national courts; a legal-aid FAQ tracks document rules.
entry_documents.interaction: Entry screening sits upstream of every later stage: a document discrepancy can become refusal, fraud referral or detention, and the division's civil-rights act cannot reach consular adjudication.

investigation_detention_custody.exposure: From 2026 the national corrections bureau adopted one state's policies mandating conversion-style treatment of trans inmates (hair cutting, hormone removal, substituted psychiatric drugs); the bureau stopped reporting trans prisoner counts from 2025. In immigration custody, trans men report forced labour, beatings, solitary confinement and severe sexual abuse.
investigation_detention_custody.protection: No division-specific custody incident is documented; the risk map itself flags shortfalls in protections for incarcerated trans people.
investigation_detention_custody.interaction: A visitor who is refused entry, overstays or is charged moves from border handling into federal custody where the hostile policies operate directly; the division's courts do not reach federal facilities.

federal_state_facilities.exposure: The Jan 2025 order bars trans people from government-funded single-sex facilities congruent with their identity, reaching airports and federal buildings a visitor uses. Four states criminalise facility use in certain circumstances; the map notes other sex-defining laws may apply beyond those shown.
federal_state_facilities.protection: No facility ban is documented for this division, which a July 2026 assessment places in a low-risk tier; its civil-rights act makes identity discrimination unlawful.
federal_state_facilities.interaction: State non-discrimination cannot cancel the federal facility rule; federal pre-emption means the visitor meets the restrictive rule wherever federal funding or ownership applies.

care_services.exposure: Federal orders describe minors' gender-affirming care as mutilation, freeze funding, and the DOJ subpoenaed under-19 hospital records in summer 2025; the July 2026 map says the division falls short on healthcare equity.
care_services.protection: Conversion therapy is banned division-wide; no division-specific care restriction or care-denial incident involving a visitor is documented.
care_services.interaction: An injured or ill traveller enters federally funded emergency care where the national posture, not the division's statute, shapes treatment and record handling.

threat_framing_law_enforcement.exposure: A Dec 2025 DOJ memo sets rewards around offences tied to 'radical gender ideology' framing; a May 2026 counterterrorism strategy prioritises groups that are 'radically pro-transgender'; a Jan 2025 order directs law enforcement to investigate 'gender ideology'. A 2025 poll found 66% back assigned-sex-on-documents laws.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.protection: Division civil-rights enforcement, explicit gender-identity hate-crime coverage from Jan 2025, abolished panic defence (2024) and a high-court pronoun ruling operate as counters.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.interaction: Federal framing raises the probability and severity of any stop, while division prosecutors and courts remain a genuine, if partial, check.

minors_guardians.exposure: Federal orders criminalise teachers facilitating a trans minor's social transition and subpoena under-19 medical records; 27 states bar minors' care (not documented here); facility bans reach K-12 schools in many units.
minors_guardians.protection: No division-specific minor restriction is documented; the 2025 athletic resolution is advisory only; division non-discrimination covers services.
minors_guardians.interaction: A visiting family meets federal facility and document rules first; division protections apply only once inside the division and do not bind federal actors.

street_violence_police_response.exposure: National bias-incident data show persistent bias reporting; four units carry 'Do Not Travel' flags for trans people (July 2026) — this division is not among them; no division-specific anti-trans violence or enforcement statistics exist in the inventory.
street_violence_police_response.protection: Explicit gender-identity hate-crime coverage, panic-defence abolition, codified non-discrimination and functioning state courts that have ruled for trans litigants.
street_violence_police_response.interaction: Strong division recourse reduces street-level exposure, but cannot remedy federal screening, facility or custody conduct.

remedies_unknowns.exposure: Multiple federal orders are blocked, enjoined or pending, so exposure changes with travel date; the inventory does not confirm which mapped ban group this division occupies, whether its IDs carry an 'X' marker, or any custody or care practice locally.
remedies_unknowns.protection: Active civil-liberties litigation, a running legal-aid FAQ, division high-court precedent and codified protections show functioning, trans-friendly state institutions.
remedies_unknowns.interaction: Open questions (visa treatment, federal facility scope, detention placement) are lighter than the documented federal exclusions but remain unresolved rather than safe.

anchor_checks.comparison: Closest analogue: no presentation offence, passports nominally accepted, but a birth-sex rule in federally funded buildings with no working remedy. Ours sits slightly higher because the division adds codified non-discrimination, explicit hate-crime coverage and a low-risk assessment — but lower than 0.55 because the federal facility rule plus visa-refusal instructions are real universal exposures, not just politeness.

0.55-B shows repeated hostile service treatment with only partial remedies and no universal rule. Our division's street and service sphere is stronger than that, yet the federal layers — entry-document scrutiny, facility exclusion, documented custody abuse — are heavier and inescapable, so the combined regime rates below it.

0.75-C offers acceptance, a dead-letter statute, enforced compensation and only an open edge case. Our dossier documents an operative federal facility exclusion and entry-refusal instructions with no remedy, plus documented custody mistreatment — materially worse on the precedence ladder, so clearly below.

0.35-D has nationwide service refusal at scale with findings but no orders. Our division does not show pervasive service denial; documented discrimination there is unlawful and litigated. That gap keeps us a full step above, despite harsher entry and custody features.

parsed.synthesis: The division and the federal regime pull in opposite directions and the combined rule is the harsher operative one at shared stages. Within the division, a trans visitor gets codified non-discrimination, explicit hate-crime coverage, a panic-defence ban and courts that have delivered for trans litigants — genuine traveller-facing protection, not merely resident machinery. But airports, federal buildings, visa adjudication, immigration custody and federal prisons are all national territory: birth-sex facility exclusion, document-based refusal with possible lifetime fraud findings, security-screening outing, and documented conversion-style treatment and abuse in custody follow the traveller regardless of the state's posture. Pending litigation makes exposure date-dependent, not absent. The division therefore sits above states with only service friction, but below any jurisdiction lacking an operative federal exclusion.
